## Train, validation and test strategy

<!-- Task 4: the chosen split and its justification; what generalisation it represents; possible leakage or optimistic performance. -->
The Siamese network and the CNN had different data-split strategies to reflect their differing tasks: Siamese was stratified by writer, while CNN was by session, but the proportion was kept the same for each - training (60%), validation (20%), and test (20%).

Siamese was split at the writer level to ensure that no writer appeared in more than one set. A random image-level split was avoided, as this would allow the same writer to appear in both training and test sets, which would artificially inflate performance and produce an optimistic estimate of the model's generalisability. Testing on unseen writers provides a more meaningful assessment of the model's ability to verify handwriting from individuals not encountered during training. This evaluation reflects how the model would perform in a real-world setting; for example, verifying whether two documents were written by the same previously unseen individual. Image pairs were constructed independently within each split to prevent images from overlapping across datasets. 

A key limitation of this strategy is the small number of writers in this dataset. With only 20 writers in total, the split allocates just four writers each to the validation and test sets, making performance estimates noisy and potentially sensitive to which writers were assigned to each set. Furthermore, the decision threshold was selected by maximising balanced accuracy on the validation set and is therefore optimised for those four specific writers, which may constitute a mild source of optimism and may not generalise perfectly to unseen writers. 

The datasets for CNN were split on session-level. Since the task was writer-identification, we had to train the model on all writers, and evaluate its performance on the sessions held out. This evaluation represents the setting of: given a set of handwritten images, how well can we classify an image given a new session? For this strategy, there is the limitation of the few sessions (3 for training, 1 for validation and 1 for testing).

For both models, the test set was kept independent and used only for final evaluation to provide an assessment of the model performance.
